title: World Cup: a Poisonous Cocktail of Spectacle, Kitsch and Patriotism
author: Mira Oklobdzija
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Science_World_in_Vancouver_during_2026_FIFA_World_Cup-680x486.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/23/world-
cup-a-poisonous-cocktail-of-spectacle-kitsch-and-patriotism/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/07/Science_World_in_Vancouver_during_2026_FIFA_World_Cup-680x486.jpg)

Photograph Source: Quintin Soloviev - [CC BY
4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)

The World Cup is a photographic image of the world, but it is overexposed. It
is blurred though the filters of nationalist propaganda and individual
heroics. At play are all the features of geopolitics: power games, big money,
troubles with AI, competition at all costs, threats, animosities, and
mistrust, to name just a few.

Consider, for instance, the Olympic Games. In the Olympic Games, the rules are
clear. No kind of demonstration or political, religious, or racial propaganda
is permitted at any Olympic sites, venues, or areas. Individuals,
organizations, and nations cannot profit from them, politically or
commercially. The goal is to promote friendly efforts and healthy rivalry.

The World Cup, by contrast, is a professional championship with its own
changing rules and an open focus on profit for all involved. The national
exaltation of the results is expected. The World Cup mobilizes nations around
their teams and, especially, around heroes on those teams. As the biggest
spectacles on the planet, aside from wars, World Cup matches would make Roman
rulers envious.

**Ritualized Spectacle**

The bigger the spectacle, the more elements of rituals they embrace. According
to Émile Durkheim, rituals create a state of collective effervescence, forging
emotional unity and reminding people they are part of something larger. That
can give individuals a warm feeling of belonging or a blinding patriotic zeal.
In _The Mass Psychology of Fascism_ , Wilhelm Reich convincingly depicted how
the energies of the masses can be steered, manipulated and exploited.

When it comes to rituals connected to sport events, “togetherness” is
demonstrated through repetitive acts, the wearing of various sorts of
uniforms, flag-waving, shouting with or without music. The “Viking row” of the
Norwegian fans leaves many impressed and others envious. Testosterone is on
open display, allowing for the free expression of basic instincts without the
label of “uncivilized.” Hero-worship also plays a prominent role, even when
the heroes are not at their best. This summer in the United States, the
[heroes have been](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7442136/2026/07/13/world-
cup-ranking-top-50-players-messi-bellingham-mbappe/ "heroes have been") Harry
Kane, Lionel Messi, Erling Haaland, Cristiano Ronaldo, Kylian Mbappe, Jude
Bellingham and others at the top of the list. . Donald Trump and FIFA chief
Gianni Infantino, though not actively chasing the ball, have tried but failed
to join their ranks.

At the margins but persistently followed by the cameras are the rich, famous,
and powerful. Many heads of states traveled to support their national teams.
Glued to their screens, spectators around the world could also follow the
socializing of David Beckham and Tom Cruise, scrutinize the national insignia
embraced by Brad Pitt and his girlfriend, wonder if Mick Jagger has lost
weight, eyeball the outfits chosen by the jaded Victoria Beckham, witness Ryan
Reynolds’s joy of cheering. and observe Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez
conversing. Who can ask for more from a sport?

Whatever else the World Cup delivers, it certainly provides a good amount of
kitsch. According to the definition, kitsch appeals to popular or lowbrow
taste, it is often of poor quality, using bright and clashing colours, is
overly dramatic, immediately grabs attention, and evokes shallow emotions. Two
steps forward is novelist Milan Kundera and his concept of “totalitarian
kitsch,” which denies the complexities, doubts, and unpleasant realities of
human existence by banning dissent, irony, and individuality. Each group of
World Cup fans shows dissent only toward the judges when they start waving
yellow or red cards at their favorites. Such fans unify against all the
others, who are also unifying against all the others. It is blind tribalism at
its best.

**Money and****P****ower**

The World Cup means money. Tickets prices are soaring. “FIFA recently listed a
ticket for the July 19 final at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium for $32,970,”
[according to Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/brettknight/2026/06/10/the-
highest-paid-players-at-the-2026-world-cup/ "according to Forbes"). “In April,
FIFA’s resale site listed four seats to the final for a little less than $2.3
million each.”. So, FIFA and the host stadiums are financially thriving, and
so are broadcasters, traveling companies, sponsors, advertisers, hotels in
America, and pubs around the world. Visitors are spending whatever they can.
And before each game, the TV audience in The Netherlands was regularly
informed that “this program has been brought to you by Coca Cola.”

Professional football has long been a big business, with players bought and
sold at high prices. This practice is called the “transfer system,” and it’s
been in effect since 1893, when the English Football Association formally
registered players as owned by their clubs. This year’s World Cup features two
hero-billionaires, Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi. Others are simply
millionaires, earning on-field salaries and off-field payments through
endorsements, licensing, appearances, and memorabilia as well as cash returns
from any businesses in which the athlete has a significant interest.

Money goes well with power. In football, Gianni Infantino (an Italian, Swiss,
and Lebanese citizen) is [worth $20
million](https://athlonsports.com/soccer/fifa-president-gianni-infantino-wife-
children-parents-ethnicity-net-worth-nationality "worth $20 million") as of
2026, plus an annual compensation as FIFA president of $6 million per year. He
also knows how to choose friends. He tirelessly and shamelessly praises Donald
Trump, awarding him the FIFA Peace Prize in a rather [tasteless political
spectacle](https://athlonsports.com/soccer/fifa-president-gianni-infantino-
wife-children-parents-ethnicity-net-worth-nationality "tasteless political
spectacle") that shouldn’t have anything to do with sport. Afterwards, after
an intimate phone call from Trump, Infantino decided that a decision of a
professional referee wouldn’t stand and American footballer Folarin Balogun
could play even after receiving a red card. For a moment Trump was happy, but
his outrageous intervention didn’t save the American team, which lost
convincingly against Belgium.

**In Other Scandals**

U.S. foreign policy also played a role in the games. Iran’s team could enter
U.S. soil only a day before each match and then had to quickly return after
the game to their accommodations in Tijuana, Mexico. U.S. Customs and Border
Protection denied Somalian referee Omar Arana entry to the country because of
some unspecified security challenge, and FIFA promptly removed him from the
tournament.

Artificial intelligence also contributed to the games this summer. Video
Assistant Referee (VAR) come under scrutiny following a string of
[controversial decisions](https://www.britannica.com/sports/Biggest-FIFA-
World-Cup-Controversies "controversial decisions") in matches involving
several countries, particularly Argentina and Portugal.

For these moves and others, FIFA and Infantino in particular lost a lot of
respect. Trump was ridiculed in virtually all corners of the globe. And
European trust in the United States and its president dropped, with 81 percent
of citizens from eight countries [considering America
unreliable](https://www.pewresearch.org/global/2026/06/23/european-views-of-
trump-and-the-u-s-are-especially-negative/ "considering America unreliable").
But this, too, was an expression of patriotism, of the anti-American variety.

The game itself remains beautiful. As Tárlach Ó Ruiséil
[writes](https://diem25.org/world-cup-2026-power-and-profit/ "writes"):

> Football is one of the greatest art forms. The ability of a player to
> manipulate their body like the finest ballet dancer, to do what appears
> unnatural—a sudden change of direction, the power of a shot or header,
> athletic grace and strength—comes together in a free-flowing orchestra at
> its very best… The best players on the biggest stage, cultivating their
> talents while inspiring national pride, have turned the World Cup into the
> most iconic sporting spectacle on earth.

Though he insists that football belongs to the people, not to oligarchs,
politicians, advertisers, or corporate executives, Ruiséil points out that the
game never lacked political significance.

> Italy’s triumphs in 1934 and 1938 were inseparable from Mussolini’s fascist
> regime. The 1978 World Cup served Argentina’s military dictatorship as a
> notorious exercise in sportswashing. And in 2026, Donald Trump’s public
> intervention… sounded less like a head of state respecting sporting
> independence and more like a powerful man expecting a favour.

**Viking Row**

The term ‘patriotism’ is generally perceived as something positive, though
much has been [written to the contrary](https://pescanik.net/terracotta-army/
"written to the contrary"). It is something more than the sense of belonging,
and its darker sides are easily overlooked. For example, and
characteristically _, Milénio Stadium_ , a Portuguese Canadian Weekly
[claims](https://mileniostadium.com/opiniao/vincent-black/global-stage-for-
soccer-patriotism/ "claims"):

> That emotional connection is what makes the FIFA World Cup one of the most
> powerful and patriotic events in the world…. (it) proves that soccer is more
> than a game—it is a powerful expression of national pride, capable of
> uniting millions in a shared sense of identity, passion, and hope.

It would be useful to elaborate more on the word “hope” in this context, but
sport commentators don’t have to be experts on all things socio-political. On
the other hand, it would be farfetched to expect equal enthusiasm from
football fans for both their team and their opponents. Their hearts go first
to their own flag and team, and only when their clubs of choice are not
playing or have been eliminated can football lovers appreciate the sport as it
should be.

Not everyone will go along with the masses and their patriotic enthusiasms.
Norwegian football fan Emil Anners Lappen
[decided](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vpk9JazWn18 "decided"), for
instance, not to row while thousands of his countrymen directly around him
did. Kundera’s totalitarian kitsch describes a political and aesthetic system
in which all answers are given in advance in such a way as to preclude any
questions. The true opponent of totalitarian kitsch is the person who asks
questions and refuses to succumb to mass sentiment, even if those feelings are
close to his heart and mind.
